E3.title: Dark matter
E3.text: However, multiple lines of evidence suggest the majority of dark matter is not baryonic:

E4.title: Dark matter
E4.text: Dark matter is not known to interact with ordinary baryonic matter and radiation except through gravity, making it difficult to detect in the laboratory.

E5.title: Dark matter
E5.text: The most prevalent explanation is that dark matter is some as-yet-undiscovered subatomic particle, such as either weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) or axions.

E6.title: Dark matter
E6.text: The other main possibility is that dark matter is composed of primordial black holes.

E8.title: Dark matter
E8.text: In 1978, Steigman et al. presented a study that extended earlier cosmological relic particle density calculations to any hypothetical stable, electrically neutral, weak-scale lepton, showing how such a particle's abundance would "freeze out" in the early Universe and providing analytic expressions that linked its mass and weak interaction cross-section to the present-day matter density.

E9.title: Dark matter
E9.text: By decoupling the analysis from specific neutrino properties and treating the candidate generically, the authors set out a framework that later became the standard template for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) and for comparing particle-physics models with cosmological constraints.

E10.title: Dark matter
E10.text: Though subsequent work has refined the methodology and explored many alternative candidates, this paper marked the first explicit, systematic treatment of dark matter as a new particle species beyond the Standard Model.

E11.title: Dark matter
E11.text: By the late 1970s the existence of dark matter halos around galaxies was widely recognized as real, and became a major unsolved problem in astronomy.

E25.title: Dark matter
section_path: Particle aggregation and dense dark matter objects
E25.text: It lacks a diversity of interactions needed to form structures

E26.title: Dark matter
E26.text: Unparticle physics – Speculative theory of non-particle matter

E27.title: Dark matter
section_path: Non-mainstream and less established particle, field, and structure theories

E28.title: Dark matter
E28.text: If dark matter is not an undiscovered particle, then the next possibility is that general relativity, the theory underpinning modern cosmology, is incorrect.

E29.title: Dark matter
E29.text: General relativity is well-tested on Solar System scales, but its validity on galactic or cosmological scales has not been well proven.

E30.title: Dark matter
E30.text: A suitable modification to general relativity can conceivably eliminate the need for dark matter.

E31.title: Dark matter
E31.text: The best-known theories of this class are modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) and its relativistic generalization tensor–vector–scalar gravity (TeVeS), f(R) gravity, negative mass, dark fluid, entropic gravity, conformal gravity, and massive gravity.

E33.title: Dark matter
E33.text: The identity of dark matter is unknown, but there are many hypotheses about what dark matter could consist of, as set out in the table below.

E34.title: Dark matter
E34.text: Mention of dark matter is made in works of fiction.

E35.title: Dark matter
E35.text: In such cases, it is usually attributed extraordinary physical or magical properties, thus becoming inconsistent with the hypothesized properties of dark matter in physics and cosmology.

E37.title: Dark matter
E37.text: Although both dark matter and ordinary matter are matter, they do not behave in the same way.

E38.title: Dark matter
E38.text: In particular, in the early universe, ordinary matter was ionized and interacted strongly with radiation via Thomson scattering.

E39.title: Dark matter
E39.text: Dark matter does not interact directly with radiation, but it does affect the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by its gravitational potential (mainly on large scales) and by its effects on the density and velocity of ordinary matter.

E40.title: Dark matter
E40.text: Ordinary and dark matter perturbations, therefore, evolve differently with time and leave different imprints on the CMB.

E41.title: Dark matter
section_path: Non-mainstream and less established particle, field, and structure theories
E41.text: Dark radiation – Postulated type of radiation that mediates interactions of dark matter

E42.title: Baryonic dark matter
E42.text: The total amount of baryonic dark matter can be inferred from models of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and observations of the cosmic microwave background.

E43.title: Baryonic dark matter
E43.text: Both indicate that the amount of baryonic dark matter is much smaller than the total amount of dark matter.

E44.title: Dark matter
E44.text: As of 2026, there has been no confirmed detection of dark matter from these standard WIMP searches.

E45.title: Dark matter
E45.text: Instead, experiments have placed strong upper limits on the particle's interaction cross-section with nucleons.

E46.title: Dark matter
E46.text: In late 2025, the LZ experiment reported the exclusion of WIMP cross-sections above 9 GeV/c2 and the first detection of boron-8 solar neutrinos via coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering in a dark matter detector.

E47.title: Dark matter
E47.text: This was the first experimental entry into the "neutrino fog", an irreducible background of neutrino interactions that mimics dark matter signals and complicates future WIMP searches.

parts.part: Dark matter is different from neutrinos.
parts.justification: The evidence suggests that dark matter has different properties and interactions than neutrinos, such as not interacting with ordinary baryonic matter and radiation except through gravity.
